qs.q: Which feature best characterises a fibroadenoma of the breast?
o: Well-circumscribed mobile rubbery mass in young women
Fixed hard mass with skin tethering in older women
Unilateral bloody nipple discharge in middle-aged women
Bilateral nodularity fluctuating with menstrual cycles
qs.e: Fibroadenoma is a well-circumscribed, firm, mobile mass (breast mouse) most common in women under 30. It is composed of both stromal and epithelial elements with no significant malignant potential.

ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Fibroadenoma is the most common benign breast tumor, occurring in young women. It is a biphasic lesion of stromal and epithelial proliferation that is hormone‑responsive and usually harmless.

sections.p: A fibroadenoma is a well‑circumscribed, mobile breast mass composed of proliferating intralobular stroma and ductal epithelium. Diagnosis relies on clinical exam, imaging, and core needle biopsy when needed.
b: Benign, biphasic tumor
Most common in women 15‑35 years
MED12 mutation in ~2/3 of cases

t.b: Is the lump firm, rubbery, mobile, and painless? Confirms typical fibroadenoma feel.
Shows a well‑defined, hypoechoic, homogeneous mass with smooth borders. Helps differentiate from cysts or malignancy.
May reveal a dense, well‑circumscribed mass; calcifications are uncommon. Absence of spiculated margins supports benign nature.
Confirms biphasic histology and excludes phyllodes tumor. If unavailable, refer for excisional biopsy if suspicion persists.

sections.p: Benign fibroadenomas are not staged; however, size (>5 cm) and rapid growth raise concern for phyllodes tumor or atypia, prompting more aggressive work‑up.
b: Small (<2 cm) – routine follow‑up
Large (>5 cm) or rapid growth – consider excision

sections.p: Fibroadenoma arises from hormonal stimulation of intralobular stroma, with genetic contribution from MED12 mutations. No infectious cause, but endocrine disorders can influence growth.
b: Estrogen excess (puberty, pregnancy)
MED12 somatic mutation
Family history of benign breast disease

sections.p: Young women notice a painless, firm, mobile lump that may enlarge during menses, pregnancy, or hormone therapy and shrink after menopause.
b: Usually solitary; can be multiple or bilateral
No skin changes, nipple discharge, or systemic symptoms

sections.p: Imaging and tissue sampling guide management, especially when size or growth pattern is atypical.

t.b: Distinguishes solid from cystic; typical fibroadenoma appears well‑circumscribed. If unavailable, clinical exam guides decision.
Used in women >30 y to assess density; lack of spiculated margins supports benignity.
Provides definitive histology; required if imaging is indeterminate or lesion >3 cm.

sections.p: Although benign, certain features suggest malignancy or a phyllodes tumor that can become aggressive.
b: Rapid increase in size over weeks
Hard, fixed, or irregular borders
Skin dimpling, nipple retraction, or ulceration

sections.p: Treatment is individualized: observation for small stable lesions, surgical excision for large, symptomatic, or atypical masses.
b: Observation with 6‑month ultrasound if <2 cm and stable
Excisional biopsy or vacuum‑assisted removal for >3 cm or growing lesions
Avoid unnecessary wide excision to preserve breast tissue

sections.p: Regular breast self‑examination and periodic imaging keep track of any change. No proven preventive drugs; hormonal balance is key.
b: Self‑exam every 3 months for young women
Ultrasound annually if multiple fibroadenomas
Counsel on avoiding unnecessary hormonal supplements

sections.p: Several other breast lesions mimic fibroadenoma clinically and radiologically.
b: Phyllodes tumor – larger, more cellular stroma, may recur
Breast cyst – fluid‑filled, transilluminates, changes with aspiration
Fibrocystic change – diffuse tenderness, multiple cysts

sections.p: Imaging and pathology can be deceptive if not interpreted in context.
b: Ultrasound may miss small areas of stromal atypia, leading to under‑diagnosis of phyllodes tumor
Core biopsy sampling error can underestimate cellularity

whenToSeekHelp: Skin changes, nipple retraction, or discharge

faq.q: Do fibroadenomas increase breast cancer risk?
faq.a: Simple fibroadenomas do not raise risk; complex fibroadenomas slightly increase risk (≈1.5‑2×).

faq.q: Can a fibroadenoma disappear on its own?
faq.a: Yes, especially after menopause; hormonal decline can cause involution.
No. Small, stable lesions are safely observed; surgery is reserved for symptomatic or atypical cases.
